questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Crossing Aa × Aa (one gene, complete dominance) gives what phenotype ratio?
questions.explain: 3 out of 4 offspring show the dominant phenotype (AA, Aa, Aa), 1 shows recessive (aa). The 1:2:1 trap is the genotype ratio, not the phenotype ratio.
questions.source: punnett-square-calculator.html, punnett('Aa','Aa') gives phe {A_:3, aa:1}, so 3:1.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with q = 0.3, what fraction of the population is heterozygous?
questions.explain: Heterozygote frequency is the 2pq term. The 0.09 trap is q squared, the recessive homozygotes, and 0.49 is p squared.
questions.source: hardy-weinberg-calculator.html, bars(p,q) with p = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7: het = 2 x 0.7 x 0.3 = 0.42.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A test cross breeds an unknown-genotype individual with:
questions.explain: Only a recessive partner contributes nothing dominant, so every offspring phenotype reads the unknown parent's gametes directly. All-dominant offspring means AA, a roughly 1:1 split means Aa.
questions.source: punnett-square-calculator.html, punnett('Aa','aa') gives phe {A_:1, aa:1} (1:1) while punnett('AA','aa') gives phe {A_:2} (all dominant).

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumptions?
choices: No new mutation at the locus
questions.explain: Equilibrium requires that nothing changes allele frequencies, so the model assumes selection is absent. Active selection is one of the forces that pushes a population off the p squared, 2pq, q squared curve.
questions.source: hardy-weinberg-calculator.html assumptions section: random mating, no mutation, no migration, no selection, large population.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Two type A parents have a type O child. Is that possible?
questions.explain: A blood test reports the phenotype, which cannot tell AA from AO. Reading a phenotype as if it were the genotype is the error behind most paternity confusion.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, GENO.A = ['AA','AO']; tally(cross('AO','AO')) gives {A:3, O:1}, so 1 in 4.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: An AB parent and an O parent can have which blood types of child?
questions.explain: The AB parent always passes A or B and the O parent always passes O, so every child is AO or BO. This is the one cross where neither parent's own type can appear in the child.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, tally(cross('AB','OO')) gives {A:2, B:2}.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: In Hardy-Weinberg, what does 2pq represent?
questions.explain: The factor of two is there because a heterozygote can be assembled two ways, a dominant egg with a recessive sperm or the reverse. Dropping it is the single most common Hardy-Weinberg slip.
questions.source: hardy-weinberg-calculator.html, bars() labels p*p as AA, 2*p*q as Aa and q*q as aa.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: If q equals 0.1 for a recessive allele, what fraction of the population are carriers?
questions.explain: Carriers are the heterozygotes, so this is the 2pq term. Note that carriers outnumber affected individuals eighteen to one here, which is why rare recessive alleles persist.
questions.source: hardy-weinberg-calculator.html, bars(0.9, 0.1): het = 2 x 0.9 x 0.1 = 0.18, q squared = 0.01.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Why are X-linked recessive conditions more common in males?
questions.explain: With a single X there is no second copy to mask a recessive allele, so one hit is enough. A female needs the allele on both X chromosomes, which is far rarer.
questions.source: x-linked-inheritance-calculator.html, maleStatus(a) returns affected on a single h, while femaleStatus needs h === 2 in recessive mode.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A dihybrid cross AaBb x AaBb gives which phenotype ratio?
questions.explain: That ratio assumes the two genes assort independently. Linked genes on the same chromosome distort it toward the parental combinations, which is how linkage was discovered.
questions.source: dihybrid-cross-calculator.html, dihybrid('AaBb','AaBb') gives phenos {A_B:9, A_b:3, a_B:3, a_b:1} over 16 boxes.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: What does a chi-square goodness of fit test compare?
choices: Two allele frequencies to each other
A genotype ratio to a phenotype ratio
One generation's counts to the next
questions.explain: The test asks whether a deviation from a predicted ratio is bigger than sampling noise. It needs raw counts, not percentages, because the sample size is what decides whether a gap matters.
questions.source: chi-square-genetics-calculator.html, calc(): e = ratio[i]/rsum*total and chi2 sums (obs - e) squared over e.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Which genotypes give an Rh positive phenotype?
questions.explain: D is dominant, so one copy is enough to put the antigen on the red cell. That is why two Rh positive parents can still have an Rh negative child, if both are carriers.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, RHG = {'+':['DD','Dd'], '-':['dd']}.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 400 people. Under Hardy-Weinberg, what fraction of the population are carriers?
questions.explain: Affected people are the q squared class, so take a square root first to get the allele frequency, then build the heterozygote term. Answering 0.05 stops at the allele frequency instead of the carrier frequency.
questions.source: q squared = 1/400 = 0.0025, so q = 0.05 and p = 0.95. hardy-weinberg-calculator.html bars(0.95, 0.05): het = 2 x 0.95 x 0.05 = 0.095, p squared = 0.9025.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A population of 500 is genotyped as 320 AA, 160 Aa and 20 aa. What is the frequency of the A allele?
questions.explain: Count alleles, not people: every homozygote contributes two copies and every heterozygote one. Answering 0.64 reports the AA genotype frequency, which is p squared rather than p.
questions.source: hardy-weinberg-calculator.html counts mode: p = (2 x 320 + 160)/(2 x 500) = 800/1000 = 0.80, and q = 0.20. Chi-square comes out at 0, so this population sits at equilibrium.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Counting 180 AA, 120 Aa and 100 aa individuals, what is q by direct allele counting?
questions.explain: Direct counting needs no equilibrium assumption, which is the point of doing it when all three genotypes are visible. The 0.50 trap is the square root of aa over N, a shortcut that is only valid at equilibrium.
questions.source: how-to-calculate-allele-frequency.html calc(400 total): q = (2 x 100 + 120)/(2 x 400) = 320/800 = 0.40, p = (2 x 180 + 120)/800 = 0.60. Its shortcut field gives sqrt(100/400) = 0.50.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: In an AaBb x AaBb dihybrid cross, what fraction of the 16 boxes are aabb?
questions.explain: Each parent makes an ab gamete one time in four, and the two events are independent, so multiply the two quarters. Answering 1/4 multiplies nothing and treats the two genes as one.
questions.source: dihybrid-cross-calculator.html, dihybrid('AaBb','AaBb') genos: aabb appears 1 time in n = 16 boxes.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A type AB parent and a type O parent. What percent of their children are expected to be type A?
questions.explain: The O parent can only pass O, so the child's type is decided entirely by which allele the AB parent sends. Half the children get A and half get B, and no child is AB or O.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, tally(cross('AB','OO')) gives {A:2, B:2} out of 4 boxes, so 50 percent type A.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: An AO parent and a BO parent. What is the chance of a type O child?
questions.explain: Only the box where both parents happen to send their O allele gives OO, and each sends O half the time. This is the cross where all four blood types are possible from one pairing.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, tally(cross('AO','BO')) gives {AB:1, A:1, B:1, O:1}, so 1 in 4 is type O.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A carrier mother and an unaffected father, X-linked recessive trait. What fraction of all their children are expected to be affected?
questions.explain: Half the sons are affected, but sons are only half the children, so the two halves multiply. Answering 50 percent quotes the risk within the sons and forgets to scale it to all children.
questions.source: x-linked-inheritance-calculator.html, mother Hh x father HY in recessive mode: sons 50 percent affected, daughters 50 percent carrier, so of all children 25 percent are affected sons.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A monohybrid cross gives 84 tall and 36 short plants. Tested against 3:1, what is the chi-square value?
questions.explain: Work out each expected count from the total first, then add one squared-difference term per class. The 3.84 trap is the critical value you compare against, not the statistic itself.
questions.source: chi-square-genetics-calculator.html, obs [84,36] against ratio [3,1]: expected 90 and 30, terms (84-90)^2/90 = 0.40 and (36-30)^2/30 = 1.20, chi2 = 1.60 with df = 1.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A pediatrician delivers a type O newborn. The mother is type A and the listed father is type AB, and he disputes paternity. What does the blood typing establish?
choices: AB passes A or B, so this man is excluded
He could still be the father if he is AO
Blood type can never exclude a father here
The typing proves he is the father
questions.explain: An AB individual has no O allele to give, so every child of his carries A or B and shows it. Exclusion is the only thing ABO typing can do well: it never confirms paternity, because millions of men share any blood type.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, GENO.AB = ['AB'] so the only pairings are AB x AA giving {A:2, AB:2} and AB x AO giving {A:2, AB:1, B:1}. No type O child appears in either.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: An Rh negative mother and an Rh positive father have an Rh positive first child. What can you say about the second child?
choices: The second child must also be Rh positive
The chance drops because one was positive
The father must be DD, so every child is positive
The chance of Rh positive is 50 to 100 percent
questions.explain: Rh positive covers both DD and Dd, and the first child being positive does not tell you which the father is, so the honest answer is a range. Each conception is independent, so no earlier child shifts the odds.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, rhOdds('-','+') returns {lo:0.5, hi:1, exact:false}: dd x DD gives 4 of 4 positive, dd x Dd gives 2 of 4.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A population of 500 has 400 AA, 50 Aa and 50 aa. A student takes the square root of 50/500 and reports q = 0.32, but counting alleles gives q = 0.15. Why do they disagree?
choices: The student should have used the 2pq term instead
Counting only works on very large samples
The square root shortcut assumes equilibrium
Both are right, they just round differently
questions.explain: Taking the root of the recessive frequency only recovers q when the genotypes already sit on the p squared, 2pq, q squared curve. Here they do not, so counting alleles is the answer and the gap between the two numbers is the evidence.
questions.source: how-to-calculate-allele-frequency.html calc(400,50,50): q = (2 x 50 + 50)/1000 = 0.15, shortcut = sqrt(50/500) = 0.316, chi-square 184.7 against a critical 3.84, so this population is far off equilibrium.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A tall plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a short plant. The 50 offspring are 28 tall and 22 short, and chi-square against 1:1 is 0.72 with df 1. What does this support?
choices: The tall parent was homozygous dominant
The data reject Mendelian inheritance here
The cross was really a 3:1 monohybrid
questions.explain: A homozygous dominant parent crossed to a recessive gives no short offspring at all, so 22 of them rules it out immediately. A chi-square of 0.72 is well under the 3.84 cutoff, so the 28 to 22 wobble is just sampling noise.
questions.source: punnett-square-calculator.html: punnett('Tt','tt') gives phe {T_:1, tt:1} while punnett('TT','tt') gives phe {T_:2}. chi-square-genetics-calculator.html on obs [28,22] against [1,1]: expected 25 each, chi2 = 0.36 + 0.36 = 0.72, df = 1.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A dihybrid cross gives 99, 27, 27 and 7 offspring in the four classes. Chi-square against 9:3:3:1 is 2.40. What is the right conclusion?
choices: The df is 4, so the test cannot be read
questions.explain: Degrees of freedom are one fewer than the number of classes, so df is 3 and the cutoff is 7.81. Failing to reject a ratio is not the same as proving it, since the test can only ever say the data are compatible.
questions.source: chi-square-genetics-calculator.html, obs [99,27,27,7] against ratio [9,3,3,1]: total 160, expected 90, 30, 30, 10, terms 0.90 + 0.30 + 0.30 + 0.90 = 2.40 with df = 3 and p = 0.494.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A colorblind man and a woman with normal vision and no family history of colorblindness have a colorblind son. Where did the son's allele come from?
choices: From his mother, who is a carrier
From a brand new mutation in his father
questions.explain: A son takes his Y from his father and his only X from his mother, so a father can never pass an X-linked allele to a son. No family history just means the carrier mothers before her happened to have no affected sons.
questions.source: x-linked-inheritance-calculator.html: mother HH x father hY gives sons 100 percent unaffected and daughters 100 percent carrier, while mother Hh x father hY gives 25 percent affected sons. A colorblind son requires an h from the mother.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A type O baby is born to a type A mother and a type B father, and the ward suspects a sample mix-up. What is the right conclusion?
choices: A type A and type B couple cannot do this at all
Both parents carry O, so 1 in 4 is type O
The baby must carry a new mutation
One parent is really type AB, not A or B
questions.explain: A and B are each dominant over O, so an AO parent and a BO parent look like plain A and B while both still carry a hidden O. This is the one parental pairing that can produce all four blood types.
questions.source: blood-type-punnett-square-calculator.html, tally(cross('AO','BO')) gives {AB:1, A:1, B:1, O:1}, so a type O child is expected 1 time in 4.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A population of 200 has 90 AA, 20 Aa and 90 aa. Chi-square against Hardy-Weinberg is 128 with df 1. What does that let you say?
choices: Natural selection is acting on this locus
The allele frequencies were computed wrong
It returns to equilibrium next generation
At least one assumption is being violated
questions.explain: The test only detects that the genotypes are off the predicted curve, never which of the five assumptions failed. A heterozygote shortfall this large usually points at non-random mating or two subpopulations sampled as one.
questions.source: hardy-weinberg-calculator.html counts mode: p = (2 x 90 + 20)/400 = 0.50, expected 50 AA, 100 Aa, 50 aa against observed 90, 20, 90, so chi2 = 32 + 64 + 32 = 128 with a critical value of 3.84.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A dihybrid test cross AaBb x aabb should give 1:1:1:1, but 100 offspring come out 45, 5, 5 and 45. Chi-square is 64 with df 3. What explains it?
choices: One of the two genes is X-linked
The two genes sit on one chromosome
A sample of 100 offspring is too small
questions.explain: The excess sits in the two parental combinations and the shortfall in the two recombinants, which is the signature of genes travelling together. A larger sample would only make the deviation more significant, not less.
questions.source: dihybrid-cross-calculator.html, dihybrid('AaBb','aabb') gives phenos {A_B:1, A_b:1, a_B:1, a_b:1}, a 1:1:1:1 expectation. chi-square-genetics-calculator.html on obs [45,5,5,45] against [1,1,1,1]: expected 25 each, four terms of 16, chi2 = 64 with df = 3.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: In a sample of 100 people, 84 show the dominant phenotype and 16 the recessive. A student reports p = 0.84. What is p actually?
questions.explain: The 84 percent lumps homozygous dominants together with heterozygotes, so it is p squared plus 2pq, not p. Start from the recessive class instead, because that is the only group whose genotype the phenotype reveals.
questions.source: q squared = 16/100 = 0.16, so q = 0.40 and p = 0.60. hardy-weinberg-calculator.html bars(0.6, 0.4) gives p squared = 0.36 and 2pq = 0.48, and 0.36 + 0.48 = 0.84, matching the observed dominant phenotype share.
